title: Circuit Theory
blurb: The electrical laws every lab is built on.

topics.name: Ohm's Law & Power
topics.question: What is Ohm's Law, and how does power follow from it
topics.assetAlt: Ohm's law and power formula wheel: the four quadrants P (watts), V (volts), I (amps) and R (ohms), each ringed by the three equivalent formulas that compute it, such as V = I × R and P = V² / R.
topics.summary: V = I·R and the power it implies.

sections.heading: The fundamental relationship
paragraphs: Voltage, current and resistance are locked together by `V = I·R`. Rearranged, it sizes a current-limiting resistor, predicts the voltage across a sensor, or confirms a wire can carry the load. Dividers, bridges and amplifier gain are all this law applied repeatedly.

sections.heading: Power dissipation
paragraphs: Power is `P = V·I = I²·R`. A resistor turns electrical energy into heat; exceed its rating and it browns, smells, and drifts. Assume 1/4 W resistors on the bench and check `I²R` before powering anything that draws real current.

topics.hint: A resistor getting hot or smelling burnt means you exceeded its 1/4 W rating — compute I²R, then raise the resistance or use a higher-wattage part before re-testing.

topics.name: Voltage Divider Rule
topics.question: How does a voltage divider turn resistance into a readable voltage
topics.assetAlt: Schematic of a two-resistor voltage divider: R1 and R2 in series across the input voltage, with the output voltage taken from the junction between them.
topics.summary: Reading resistive sensors as a voltage.

sections.heading: Splitting a voltage
paragraphs: Two series resistors split the supply: `Vout = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2)`. Almost every resistive sensor here — the LDR, the thermistor, the soil probe — is read by making it one leg of a divider and watching how Vout moves as its resistance changes.

sections.heading: Choosing the fixed resistor
paragraphs: Pick the fixed resistor near the sensor's mid-range resistance so the output swings across the widest part of the ADC range. A poor choice squashes your signal into a handful of counts.

topics.hint: An ADC reading pinned at 0 or 1023 means the fixed resistor is mismatched to the sensor — measure the sensor at both extremes and choose a fixed resistor in between.

topics.name: Pull-up / Pull-down
topics.question: Why does a digital input need a pull-up or pull-down resistor
topics.assetAlt: Side-by-side schematics of pull-up and pull-down wiring: in the pull-up, a resistor ties the input pin to +5 V and a switch pulls it to ground; in the pull-down, the resistor ties the pin to ground and the switch connects it to +5 V.
topics.summary: Giving a floating input a defined state.

sections.heading: Why inputs float
paragraphs: A digital input wired to nothing is "floating" — it picks up noise and reads randomly. A pull-up ties it to 5 V (reads HIGH until a switch pulls it LOW); a pull-down ties it to ground.

sections.heading: On the Arduino
paragraphs: Skip the external resistor with `pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP)`, which enables the internal pull-up. The logic then inverts: a pressed/closed switch reads LOW.

topics.hint: A switch that reads erratically when untouched is floating — enable INPUT_PULLUP (or add a 10 kΩ pull resistor) and invert your logic test.

topics.name: Wheatstone Bridge
topics.question: How does a Wheatstone bridge resolve a tiny resistance change
topics.assetAlt: Wheatstone bridge schematic: four resistors P, Q, R and S arranged in a diamond, a galvanometer G bridging the two middle nodes, and a battery E driving the outer corners.
topics.summary: Turning a small ΔR into a differential voltage.

sections.heading: The balanced bridge
paragraphs: Four resistors in a diamond give zero differential output when `R1/R2 = R4/R3`. Replace one arm with a sensing element and a tiny resistance change unbalances the bridge, producing a small differential voltage proportional to that change.

sections.heading: Quarter, half, full
paragraphs: Using one active arm (quarter), two (half), or all four (full) trades complexity for sensitivity and temperature compensation. The strain-gauge load cell is the canonical application.

topics.hint: A bridge output of only a few millivolts buried in noise is expected — null the offset to ≈0 V at rest first, then amplify with an op-amp stage before reading it.

topics.name: Op-Amp Gain
topics.question: How does an op-amp amplify a weak signal to a readable range
topics.assetAlt: Schematics of the two classic op-amp gain configurations: a non-inverting amplifier with gain Av = 1 + R2/R1 and an inverting amplifier with gain Av = −R2/R1, each showing its R1–R2 feedback network.
topics.summary: Setting gain and respecting the rails.

sections.heading: Setting the gain
paragraphs: A non-inverting amplifier has gain `G = 1 + Rf/Rin`; an inverting one has `G = −Rf/Rin`. This lifts millivolt bridge or sensor signals to a volt-level range the ADC can resolve.

sections.heading: Rails and offset
paragraphs: A single-supply op-amp only outputs between its rails (0–5 V here), so centre your signal and watch for clipping. Input offset voltage gets amplified too — trim or reference it deliberately.

topics.hint: An output stuck at a supply rail means the gain is too high for the input swing, or a DC offset is being amplified into saturation — reduce gain and bias the signal to re-centre it.

topics.name: PWM & Duty Cycle
topics.question: How does PWM fake an analog level with a square wave
topics.assetAlt: Three stacked waveforms illustrating pulse-width modulation: a smooth modulating signal, a constant-width pulsed carrier, and the resulting PWM signal whose pulse widths vary to track the modulating signal.
topics.summary: Duty cycle as an average voltage.

sections.heading: Duty cycle = average
paragraphs: PWM switches a pin fully on/off fast; the fraction of time it is HIGH (duty cycle) sets the effective average voltage. `analogWrite(pin, 0..255)` maps to 0–100% duty, driving LED brightness, motor speed and heater power efficiently.

sections.heading: Frequency matters
paragraphs: The right frequency depends on the load. A servo expects a specific ≈50 Hz pulse train, not the default analogWrite frequency — which is why you use the Servo library to position it.

topics.hint: A servo buzzing or refusing to hold position is getting the wrong PWM frequency — use the Servo library (correct ≈50 Hz, 1–2 ms pulse) rather than analogWrite.

topics.name: Resistors and LED Polarity
topics.question: Which resistor goes where, and why does LED orientation matter
topics.summary: Choosing the right resistor for each job and orienting the LED correctly.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: The divider uses a 4.7 kΩ resistor. The LED path uses 220 Ω to limit current. An LED is polarized, so orientation matters.

topics.hint: A reversed LED may stay off; an LED without current limiting can be damaged.
